title: Performance
summary: Write queries the optimizer loves, code that never blows a limit, and UIs that load only what you need.

lessons.title: Limits You Must Know Cold
lessons.objective: Identify inefficiencies in code and how to resolve them (governor limits per transaction)

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Many companies share the same Salesforce servers. So every **transaction** (one full run of work, like one Save click) gets a fixed **budget**. Spend too much of anything and Salesforce stops you with a `LimitException`. Nothing is saved. Limits stop one greedy job from slowing everyone else.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Think of a field trip with a strict allowance: 100 snack tokens, 150 ride tickets. Run out and your trip ends right there. Where it breaks: a kid can borrow more. Apex can't. There is no way to get extra budget mid-run.

cards.title: The numbers (per transaction)
items: SOQL queries (database reads): **100** sync / **200** async
Rows read by SOQL: **50,000** in both
DML statements (saves): **150** | DML rows: **10,000**
CPU time: **10,000 ms** sync / **60,000 ms** async
Heap (memory): **10 MB** sync / **25 MB** async (older guides say 6 / 12 MB)
Callouts: **100** | SOSL: **20** queries, **2,000** rows each

cards.title: What async changes
cards.body: **Async** Apex runs later, in the background: Batch, Queueable, `@future`. It raises just three limits. SOQL goes from 100 to 200. Heap goes from 10 MB to 25 MB. CPU goes from 10,000 ms to 60,000 ms. DML (150), query rows (50,000) and callouts (100) **stay the same**.

cards.title: What counts as CPU
cards.body: **CPU time** is time your code spends thinking. Loops, string building, JSON parsing and nested loops all count. Time spent waiting on the **database does not** count. Waiting for a callout to answer doesn't count either.

cards.title: Check before you spend
cards.body: This checks your budget first: `getX()` is what you used so far, `getLimitX()` is the cap here.
Wrapping code in `try/catch` does **not** save you. A `LimitException` can't be caught, and the whole transaction rolls back. Plan to stay under the limit, never to recover from it.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Async gets a bigger brain, not bigger hands."** Brain = queries, memory and thinking time (SOQL, heap, CPU). Hands = saves, rows and callouts. Those stay the same.

terms.say: One full run of work, start to finish, like everything one Save click starts. It all saves together, or nothing saves.
Hard caps on what one transaction may use, like queries or memory. Many companies share the servers, so the caps keep it fair.
The error when code goes over a limit. It can't be caught. Everything stops, and nothing from that run is saved.
How Apex asks the database for records. You get 100 queries per transaction, or 200 when the code runs async.
Code that saves changes: insert, update, delete and more. You get 150 DML statements per transaction, sync or async.
Time your code spends thinking, like loops and building text. Waiting for the database or a callout doesn't count.
The memory your code uses to hold data while it runs. Like desk space: 10 MB, or 25 MB when async.
When Apex calls another system over the internet. You get up to 100 per transaction.
Code that runs later, in the background, not while the user waits. Batch, Queueable and @future are kinds. It gets more SOQL, heap and CPU.

lessons.title: Bulkify or Bust
lessons.objective: Identify inefficiencies in code and how to resolve them (bulkification, collections)

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **trigger** (code that runs by itself when records are saved) gets up to **200 records at once**. If your code queries once per record, 200 records means 200 queries. The limit is 100. So it crashes at record 101. **Bulkifying** means a few queries handle any number of records.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Think of cooking 200 recipes. You don't drive to the store once per recipe. You write one shopping list, shop once, then cook at home. Bulk code works the same way: gather first, query once, then work in memory.

cards.title: The bulk recipe
items: 1. Loop: **collect** Ids into a Set
2. Run **one** query outside the loop
3. Build a **Map** for fast lookups
4. Loop again: change records in memory
5. Run **one** DML on a List

cards.title: Map from a query
cards.body: This gathers every Account Id, runs one query, and lets the Map constructor key the results by Id.

cards.title: SOQL for loop = heap saver
cards.body: This reads Cases in chunks of 200, so the whole result never sits in memory at once.

cards.title: One save, no repeats
cards.body: Save once at the end, on a List or on `map.values()`. A **Map keyed by Id** also drops duplicates, so you never hit "Duplicate id in list". Need totals? Let an **aggregate query** do the math: `SUM(Amount) ... GROUP BY AccountId`. Nested loops matching records? Use a Map lookup instead.

cards.title: Reusable code rules
items: Redefining a parent's `virtual` method needs the `override` keyword
Inner classes go only **one level** deep
Many versions of one job? An **interface** plus one class each, picked with `Type.forName()`
One **selector** class owns each object's queries and field list

cards.body: A SOQL for loop saves **heap** (memory), not **rows**. Every row still counts toward the **50,000** limit. And `@future` per record is no fix: only **50** future calls are allowed per transaction.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"No Q in the loop, no D in the loop."** No Queries and no DML inside a for loop. Ever.

terms.say: Code that runs by itself when records are saved. It can get up to 200 records at once, so it must handle them all together.
Writing code so a few queries and saves handle any number of records. Never one query or save per record.
A collection that keeps each value only once. Great for gathering Ids with no repeats.
Pairs of a key and a value, like a phone book. Give it an Id, get the record back fast, no loop needed.
Code that saves changes: insert, update, delete. Max 150 per transaction, so save a whole List at once.
A loop that reads query results in chunks of 200. It uses less memory, but every row still counts toward the 50,000 limit.
The memory your code uses while it runs. Load too much at once and the run stops.
A query that does the math in the database, like SUM or COUNT. You get the totals back, not every record.
A list of methods a class promises to have. Every class that signs it can be swapped for another.
A way to run a method later, in the background. Only 50 calls per transaction, so never one per record.

lessons.title: Selective Queries & Indexes
lessons.objective: Identify performance issues and mitigation techniques for SOQL queries on large data volumes

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Searching a huge table row by row is slow. An **index** is a sorted shortcut list for one field, so the database jumps straight to matches. A query is **selective** when an indexed filter narrows the rows below a set threshold. Then the **optimizer** (the part that decides how to run your query) uses the index.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Think of the index at the back of a textbook. Looking up "volcano" is quick. But if the word is on half the pages, you'd just read the whole book. Salesforce thinks the same way: too many matches, and it skips the index and scans everything.

cards.title: Indexed out of the box
items: `Id`, `Name`, `OwnerId`
`CreatedDate`, `SystemModstamp`
`RecordTypeId`
Lookup and master-detail fields
External ID and unique fields

cards.title: Thresholds (single filter)
items: **Standard** index: under **30%** of the first 1M rows + **15%** beyond, max **1,000,000**
**Custom** index: under **10%** of the first 1M rows + **5%** beyond, max **333,333**

cards.title: Worked example
cards.body: Take 2,000,000 rows and a **custom** index. Threshold = 10% of the first 1M (100,000) + 5% of the next 1M (50,000) = **150,000**. A filter matching 250,000 rows is not selective. With a standard index it would be 300,000 + 150,000 = 450,000.

cards.title: Need a custom index?
cards.body: Mark a field **External ID** or **Unique** and Salesforce indexes it for you. For other fields, ask **Salesforce Support**. Formula fields can be indexed only if they are **deterministic** (same inputs, same answer, every time). `TODAY()`, other objects' fields and `TEXT()` on a picklist all rule that out.

cards.title: `AND` vs `OR`
cards.body: With `AND`, one selective indexed filter can be enough. With `OR`, **every** field in the `OR` must be indexed, or no index is used. Fix it two ways: index the other field, or split it into two selective queries and merge the results in Apex.

In a **trigger**, a non-selective query on an object with **more than 200,000 records** throws **"Non-selective query against large object type"**. Adding `ORDER BY` or `LIMIT` doesn't fix it. Only a selective indexed filter does.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"30-15 standard, 10-5 custom."** Caps: **1,000,000** standard, **333,333** custom. Standard indexes get three times the room.

terms.say: A sorted shortcut list for one field. The database jumps straight to matches instead of reading every row.
A query is selective when an indexed filter keeps the matches small enough. Then the index gets used, and it's fast.
The part of Salesforce that decides how to run your query. It picks the cheapest way: use an index, or read every row.
The most rows a filter may match and still count as selective. Go over it, and the index is skipped.
The part of a query that says which rows you want, like WHERE Status = 'Open'.
A field that holds a record's Id from another system. Marking a field External ID makes Salesforce index it for you.
Same inputs, same answer, every time. A formula using TODAY() isn't, because its answer changes each day. Only deterministic formulas can be indexed.
A query whose filters match too many rows to use an index. In a trigger on an object over 200,000 records, it throws an error.

lessons.title: Query Plan & Index Killers
lessons.objective: Identify performance issues and mitigation techniques for SOQL queries (Query Plan tool, optimizer behavior)

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Before a query runs, Salesforce weighs a few ways to run it and picks the cheapest. The **Query Plan** tool shows you those options. Turn it on in Developer Console preferences. Each plan gets a **Cost** score. So you know, before you deploy, whether your query will use an index.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Think of a map app showing three routes. It picks the fastest one. The Query Plan is that route screen for your query. Where it breaks: Cost is not minutes or seconds. It's a relative score, and 1 is the line that matters.

cards.title: Reading the plan
cards.body: **Cost below 1 = selective.** Above 1 = not selective. Lower is better. The optimizer always runs the **lowest-cost** plan, even a scan. Check **Leading Operation Type**: "Index" means it uses an index. "TableScan" means it reads every row.

cards.title: Index killers
items: Negative operators: `!=`, `NOT IN`, `EXCLUDES`
Leading wildcard: `LIKE '%corp'` (trailing `LIKE 'Acme%'` is fine)
Comparing to `null` on a custom-indexed field
Non-deterministic formula fields, like ones using `TODAY()`
An `OR` where any branch is unindexed

cards.title: Fixing a killer
cards.body: Turn negatives into positives: `Status__c != 'Closed'` becomes `Status__c IN ('New', 'Working')`. Swap a `TODAY()` formula filter for a range on the **real date field**. Store a default value instead of null.
Custom indexes **skip null values** by default. So `WHERE Region__c = null` can't use the custom index, unless Support builds one that includes nulls.

cards.title: Skinny tables
cards.body: A **skinny table** is a narrow copy of one object's most-used fields, standard and custom together. That skips a database join, so reads get faster. Only **Salesforce Support** can create one. The platform keeps it in sync. Up to **100 columns**. It leaves out soft-deleted records.
Skinny tables **can't** hold fields from other objects, like the parent Account's Region. And they copy over automatically only to **Full** sandboxes.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Under 1, it runs. Over 1, it's done."** The three big killers: **NOT, %start and null**.

terms.say: A Developer Console tool that shows the ways Salesforce could run your query, and what each costs. Check it before you deploy.
A score for how heavy a plan is. Not seconds. Below 1 means selective, above 1 means not.
The plan column that says how the query starts. Index means it uses an index. TableScan means it reads every row.
Reading every single row, one by one, with no index. Slow on big tables.
Filters that say what you don't want, like != or NOT IN. They can't use an index well, so list what you do want.
A % at the start of a LIKE search, like '%corp'. The index can't help, so every row gets checked. A % at the end is fine.
Empty: no value at all. Custom indexes leave out empty values by default, so a filter on null can't use them.
A formula whose answer can change even with the same inputs, like one using TODAY(). It can't be indexed.
A narrow copy of one object's most-used fields, kept in sync by Salesforce. Reads skip combining tables, so they're faster. Only Support can create one.

lessons.title: Large Data Volumes & Skew
lessons.objective: Identify performance issues and mitigation techniques for large data volumes (data skew, sharing, loading)

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Large data volumes** (LDV) means millions of records. Trouble starts when too many records pile onto **one** owner or **one** parent. That pile-up is called **data skew**. Salesforce flags it at about **10,000 records** per owner or parent.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Think of one checkout lane with 10,000 shoppers. Everyone waits for the same cashier. Spread them over many lanes and the lines move. Skew is that one crowded lane.

cards.title: Three flavors of skew
items: **Ownership skew**: one user owns more than 10,000 records of an object
**Parent-child (account) skew**: one Account has more than 10,000 children
**Lookup skew**: huge numbers of records point to one lookup record

cards.title: Why it hurts
cards.body: Saving a child record briefly **locks its parent**. Many parallel saves on one parent fight over that lock. You get `UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW`. Moving a skewed owner in the **role hierarchy** (the org chart that controls who sees what) forces a huge **sharing recalculation**.

cards.title: The fixes
items: Skewed owner: **no role**, or a lone role at the **top** of the hierarchy
Skewed parent: **spread** children, about 10,000 or fewer each
Big reorg: **Defer Sharing Calculations**, then recalculate once

cards.title: Huge loads, extracts and deletes
items: Load with **Bulk API 2.0**, sorted by **parent Id**
Locks persist? Switch to **serial mode**
Huge extract? **PK chunking** splits by Id range (default 100,000, max 250,000)
Deleted rows sit in the Recycle Bin **15 days**; for 1M+ deletes use **hard delete**

cards.title: Big Objects
cards.body: Billions of rows that rarely change, like audit history? Use **Big Objects**. You query them by their **index fields** only, in order.
Master-detail does **not** fix parent locks. Its children lock the parent too. And more parallel batches make lock errors **worse**, not better.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"10k is the line."** One owner or one parent past 10,000 records? Spread it out.

terms.say: Large data volumes: millions of records. At that size, slow queries, locks and sharing changes start to hurt.
Too many records piled on one owner or one parent, about 10,000 or more. Like one checkout lane with every shopper.
One user owns more than 10,000 records of one object. Moving that user in the role hierarchy makes sharing recalculate for all of them.
Huge numbers of records point to the same record through a lookup field. Saves all touch that one record, so they wait in line.
The error when a save waits too long for a record another save has locked. Common when many saves hit one parent.
Salesforce rechecking who may see which records. With millions of records it can take a very long time.
Pausing sharing recalculation during big changes. When you're done, it runs once, instead of after every change.
Bulk API batches run one at a time, not side by side. Slower, but saves stop fighting over the same lock.
Splitting a huge extract into pieces by Id range. Each piece is its own quick query.
Storage for billions of rows that rarely change, like history. You can only filter on their index fields, in order.

lessons.title: Cache It, Don't Re-Fetch It
lessons.objective: Identify inefficiencies in code and how to resolve them (caching, describes, CPU)

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Fetching the same data again and again wastes queries, callouts and CPU. **Caching** means keeping a copy close by, so the next read is instant. Apex has two tools. **Static variables** last one transaction. **Platform Cache** lasts across transactions.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A static variable is a sticky note on your desk: handy all day, binned tonight. **Org cache** is the office whiteboard: everyone reads it. **Session cache** is your own notebook. Where it breaks: the whiteboard can be wiped any time. Always check it's still there.

cards.title: Static lazy-load
cards.body: This queries the rates on the first call only, then hands every later caller in the transaction the same map.

cards.title: Platform Cache
items: **Org cache**: shared by all users, across transactions, kept up to 48 hours
**Session cache**: one user's session, up to 8 hours
Both live in **partitions** you set up in Setup
Key format: `local.Partition.key` (`local` = your org's namespace)
Each item: max **100 KB**; key: max 50 characters

cards.title: Handle the miss
cards.body: This reads the rate from the cache, and on a miss fetches it and stores it for 3,600 seconds.

cards.title: Let Salesforce load it
cards.body: Implement `Cache.CacheBuilder` and Salesforce handles misses for you. Write a **non-static** `doLoad(String var)` method. `Cache.Org.get(MyClass.class, key)` calls it only when the value is missing. You never call `put()` yourself.

cards.title: CPU savers
items: Map lookups instead of **nested loops**
Describe once: skip repeated `Schema.getGlobalDescribe()`, use `Account.SObjectType.getDescribe()` and cache it
Stop **trigger recursion** with a `static Set<Id>` of processed records
Remove heavy `System.debug` calls in loops

cards.body: Session cache is **not available in async Apex** (batch, future). Use org cache there. And statics reset every transaction, so they can't share data between users.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Sticky note, whiteboard, notebook.** Static = one transaction. Org = everyone. Session = one user. Always handle the miss.

terms.say: Keeping a copy of data close by, so the next read is instant. No new query or callout needed.
Variables that last for one whole transaction, shared by all code in that run. Then they're wiped.
Salesforce memory that keeps data between transactions. Faster than fetching again, but it can be cleared any time.
Platform Cache shared by all users. An item can stay up to 48 hours.
Platform Cache for one user's session. Lasts up to 8 hours. Not available in async Apex.
A named section of Platform Cache, set up in Setup. Each one gets its own share of space.
You look in the cache and the item isn't there. So you fetch it again and put it back.
An interface you implement so Salesforce fills the cache for you. On a miss, it calls your doLoad method to get the value.
A trigger that makes itself run again by saving the same records. A static Set of done Ids stops the loop.
A loop inside a loop. 1,000 times 1,000 is a million steps. A Map lookup is much faster.

lessons.title: Snappy Lightning Web Components
lessons.objective: Identify common performance issues for user interfaces and techniques to resolve them

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A slow page usually calls the server too often, loads too much data, or builds parts nobody sees. Fast **Lightning web components** (LWC, Salesforce's modern UI building blocks) ask for less, ask less often, and reuse what they already have.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Think of a good waiter. They don't run to the kitchen after every word. They wait until you finish ordering. They bring each dish when you're ready for it. That's **debouncing** and **lazy loading**.

cards.title: Cacheable Apex
cards.body: Marking the method `cacheable=true` lets `@wire` call it and lets the browser reuse its results.

cards.title: Lightning Data Service
cards.body: For single records, use **LDS** (Lightning Data Service): `lightning-record-form`, `getRecord` and the other adapters. All components share **one cache**, and you need **no Apex**.

cards.title: Load less, later
items: `lwc:if` builds heavy parts only when needed; CSS hiding still builds them
**Pagination** or **infinite loading** instead of thousands of rows
Request only the **fields you show**
**Debounce** typing (about 300 ms) before calling Apex
Heavy getters rerun every render: compute once, store the result

cards.title: Infinite loading
cards.body: `loadMore` fetches and adds the next page; set `isLoading` while it works, and switch infinite loading off when a page comes back short.

cards.title: Sharing code
items: LWC: put shared JS in a **service component**; import with braces for a named export
Aura: one `extends`, many `implements`
An Aura base component shows child markup only where it has `{!v.body}`
Aura interfaces hold attributes, events and methods only

cards.body: A `cacheable=true` method **can't do DML**. After data changes, call `refreshApex()` with the whole value the wire gave you, not the data you copied from it.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: `OFFSET` **stops at 2,000.** For deep paging use **keyset**: `WHERE Id > :lastId ORDER BY Id LIMIT 50`. Think: a bookmark, not a page number.

terms.say: Lightning web components: Salesforce's modern building blocks for screens. Each one is a small piece of a page.
Waiting until typing stops, about 300 ms, before calling the server. One call, not one per key.
Loading a part only when it's needed, not everything up front.
Marks an Apex method as read-only, so its results can be saved and reused. Needed for @wire. It can't save changes.
Connects a component to data. It fetches the data for you and fetches again when its inputs change.
Lightning Data Service. Reads and saves single records with no Apex. All components share one cache, so they show the same data.
Builds a part of the page only when its condition is true. Hiding a part with CSS still builds it.
Loading more rows when the user scrolls to the bottom, instead of thousands at once.
Asks wired Apex data to fetch fresh results after a change. Pass it the whole value the wire gave you.
Paging by remembering the last Id you saw, then asking for the ones after it. Works past OFFSET's 2,000 limit.

lessons.title: Visualforce on a Diet
lessons.objective: Identify common performance issues for user interfaces and techniques to resolve them (Visualforce)

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Visualforce** is Salesforce's older page framework. Each time a form posts back, the page carries its **view state** (a saved copy of the controller's data). The max size is **170 KB**. Big view state means slow pages and errors. Your job is to keep it small.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Think of a backpack you carry to class every day. Pack only what you need. Leave the encyclopedia at home and look things up when you must. That's `transient`. Where it breaks: there is no bigger backpack. 170 KB is fixed.

cards.title: `transient`
cards.body: This keeps `bigList` out of view state, so you rebuild it on each request; `selectedId` is still saved.

cards.title: Shrink the page
items: Mark derived or big data `transient`
Paginate with `StandardSetController`
Query only the **fields** and rows you show
Use **one** `apex:form` where possible
Prefer `apex:outputPanel` + `rerender` over full reloads

cards.title: `readOnly="true"`
cards.body: Set it on `apex:page` and the page can read **1,000,000** query rows instead of 50,000. Iteration components can show **10,000** items. The catch: the page **can't do DML**.

cards.title: Continuations in Visualforce
cards.body: A **Continuation** lets a page wait for a slow callout without tying up the server. While it waits, the controller is saved. That **controller state** has its own **80 KB** limit, apart from view state. Transient fields help here too.

cards.title: Testing a Continuation
cards.body: Normal mocks don't run the callback. Use `Test.setContinuationResponse(label, res)` to give a fake response. Then `Test.invokeContinuationMethod(controller, con)` runs the callback.
You **can't** raise the 170 KB view state limit. Not even Support can. Also, transient data is `null` after a postback, so re-query it when you need it.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"170 to carry, transient to spare."** Find the heaviest variables in the **View State** tab of the Development Mode footer.

terms.say: Salesforce's older way to build pages, with a page plus an Apex controller behind it.
A saved copy of the controller's data, carried with the page on every postback. Max 170 KB, and it can't be raised.
When a form sends the page back to the server, like on a button click. The view state rides along.
A keyword that keeps a variable out of view state. It isn't saved, so it's null after a postback. Rebuild it when needed.
A built-in controller for lists of records. It pages through them for you, a few at a time.
A way for a page to wait for a slow callout without tying up the server. A callback runs when the answer arrives.
The controller's data saved while a Continuation waits. It has its own 80 KB limit, apart from view state.
The method that runs when the slow callout's answer comes back.
In a test, gives the Continuation a fake answer, since real callouts can't run in tests.
In a test, runs the callback method for you, because it won't run on its own.

lessons.title: Right Query, Right Place
lessons.objective: Identify performance issues and mitigation techniques for queries and long-running processes (SOSL vs SOQL, aggregates, async)

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Every job has a best tool. Searching text, adding up numbers, mixing record types and waiting on slow servers each have one. Picking the right tool saves queries, memory and time.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Think of a library. **SOSL** is the search computer: type a word, get hits from every shelf. **SOQL** is asking the librarian for one exact book. An **aggregate** is asking "how many books?" instead of carrying them all to your desk.

cards.title: SOSL vs SOQL
items: **SOSL**: text search across **many objects** at once, using the search index
**SOQL**: exact filters on **known fields** of one object (plus related ones)
SOSL returns at most **2,000** rows per query

cards.title: Aggregate instead of looping
cards.body: This lets the database add up Amount per Account and send back one row each.

cards.title: Polymorphic `TYPEOF`
cards.code:
SELECT Id, Subject,
  TYPEOF What
    WHEN Account THEN Name, Phone
    WHEN Opportunity THEN Name, Amount
  END
FROM Task
cards.body: This picks different fields depending on which object type `What` points to, all in one query.

cards.title: Offload heavy work
items: **Queueable**: chainable, takes objects, can do callouts
**Batch Apex**: millions of rows, fresh limits per chunk
**Platform Events**: decouple; the subscriber runs in its own transaction
`@future`: simple, primitives only, returns nothing

cards.title: Continuations (wait for slow callouts)
items: Up to **3** callouts each, run **in parallel**; max timeout **120 seconds**
The callback runs **once**, after all responses, in the same class
Apex: `@AuraEnabled(continuation=true)`; LWC imports from `@salesforce/apexContinuation`
**No DML** in the method that returns the Continuation; the callback may
Cacheable? Then every method in the chain must be

cards.body: `TYPEOF` **can't** be used with `GROUP BY` or `HAVING`, can't be nested, and isn't supported in **Bulk API** queries.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Search with S, select with Q, sum in the database."** Slow callout from a page? **Continuation**: 3 at once, 120 seconds tops.

terms.say: Salesforce's text search. Type a word, get matches from many objects at once. Up to 2,000 rows per search.
Asking for exact records by their field values, like WHERE Name = 'Acme'. One main object, plus related ones.
Letting the database do the math, like SUM or COUNT. You get one answer row per group, not every record.
Lets one query pick different fields depending on what kind of record a field points to, like an Account or an Opportunity.
Async Apex you can chain: one job starts the next. It can take objects, not just simple values, and can make callouts.
Async Apex for huge jobs. It splits records into chunks, and each chunk gets its own fresh limits.
Messages one part of the system sends and others listen for. The listener runs in its own transaction.
The simplest async Apex. It takes only simple values, like Ids or text, and returns nothing.
A way to wait for slow callouts without tying up the server. Up to 3 at once, 120 seconds max.
The method that runs once, after all of a Continuation's answers come back. It may save changes.

flashcards.front: How many SOQL queries can one transaction run?
flashcards.back: 100 in synchronous Apex, 200 in asynchronous Apex. That is per transaction.

flashcards.front: How many rows can SOQL read in one transaction?
flashcards.back: 50,000 rows in total. Async Apex gets no more: it is 50,000 for both.

flashcards.front: How many saves can one transaction do?
flashcards.back: 150 DML statements, touching at most 10,000 rows in total.

flashcards.front: How much CPU time does a transaction get?
flashcards.back: 10,000 ms synchronous, 60,000 ms asynchronous. Time spent in the database does not count.

flashcards.front: How much memory (heap) does a transaction get?
flashcards.back: 10 MB synchronous, 25 MB asynchronous, per current docs. Older study guides say 6 MB / 12 MB.

flashcards.front: How many callouts can one transaction make?
flashcards.back: 100 callouts, with a 120-second total timeout across all of them.

flashcards.front: How do you check how many queries you have left?
flashcards.back: Compare `Limits.getQueries()` (used so far) with `Limits.getLimitQueries()` (the cap for this context).

flashcards.front: Can `try/catch` save you from a `LimitException`?
flashcards.back: No. A `LimitException` can't be caught. The whole transaction rolls back.

flashcards.front: When is a standard-indexed filter selective?
flashcards.back: When it matches under 30% of the first 1M rows plus 15% of rows beyond that. Never more than 1,000,000 rows.

flashcards.front: When is a custom-indexed filter selective?
flashcards.back: When it matches under 10% of the first 1M rows plus 5% of rows beyond that. Never more than 333,333 rows.

flashcards.front: Which fields are indexed without asking anyone?
flashcards.back: `Id`, `Name`, `OwnerId`, `CreatedDate`, `SystemModstamp` and `RecordTypeId`. Also lookup, master-detail, External ID and unique fields.

flashcards.front: How can you index a custom field yourself?
flashcards.back: Mark it External ID or Unique. Any other field needs Salesforce Support.

flashcards.front: What does the Cost in the Query Plan tool tell you?
flashcards.back: Below 1 means selective, so an index can help. Above 1 means not selective. Lower is better.

flashcards.front: Which filters stop an index from being used?
flashcards.back: Negative operators (`!=`, `NOT IN`, `EXCLUDES`) and leading wildcards like `LIKE '%x'`.

flashcards.front: Can a custom index find null values?
flashcards.back: Not by default. Custom indexes skip nulls, so `= null` can't use them unless Support adds nulls.

flashcards.front: What is a skinny table?
flashcards.back: A narrow copy of one object's most-used fields, so reads skip a join. Built by Support, kept in sync, up to 100 columns.

flashcards.front: When does a trigger throw a non-selective query error?
flashcards.back: When a trigger runs a non-selective SOQL query on an object with more than 200,000 records.

flashcards.front: When does one owner cause ownership skew?
flashcards.back: When one user owns more than about 10,000 records of one object.

flashcards.front: How do you fix ownership skew?
flashcards.back: Give the owner no role, or a lone role at the top of the hierarchy. Spread ownership across users if you can.

flashcards.front: Why do big loads hit `UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW`?
flashcards.back: Parallel batches update children of the same parent, so they fight over its lock. Sort the file by parent Id or use serial mode.

flashcards.front: How is org cache different from session cache?
flashcards.back: Org cache is shared by all users across sessions. Session cache belongs to one user's session (max 8 hours) and doesn't work in async Apex.

flashcards.front: How long does a static variable keep its value?
flashcards.back: One transaction only. Perfect for loading data once and reusing it within that transaction.

flashcards.front: What must an Apex method have so `@wire` can call it?
flashcards.back: `@AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)`. Because results are cached, the method can't do DML.

flashcards.front: How do you refresh wired Apex data after a change?
flashcards.back: Call `refreshApex()` with the value the wire provisioned.

flashcards.front: How far can SOQL `OFFSET` skip?
flashcards.back: 2,000 rows at most. For deeper paging use keyset paging: `WHERE Id > :lastId`.

flashcards.front: How big can Visualforce view state get?
flashcards.back: 170 KB, and it can't be raised. Shrink it with `transient`, pagination and fewer fields.

flashcards.front: What does `readOnly="true"` on `apex:page` do?
flashcards.back: It raises query rows to 1,000,000 and iteration items to 10,000. The page can't do any DML.

flashcards.front: When should you use SOSL instead of SOQL?
flashcards.back: When you search text across several objects or fields and don't know where the match lives.

flashcards.front: What does `TYPEOF` do in SOQL?
flashcards.back: It picks different fields depending on which object a polymorphic lookup like `Task.What` points to.

flashcards.front: Which formula fields can be indexed?
flashcards.back: Only deterministic ones. No `TODAY()` or `NOW()`, no fields from other objects, no `TEXT()` on a picklist.

flashcards.front: Why are queries slow after a mass delete?
flashcards.back: Deleted rows sit in the Recycle Bin for 15 days, and queries must skip them. For 1M+ deletes, use Bulk API hard delete.

flashcards.front: How many callouts can one Continuation make, and how long can it wait?
flashcards.back: Up to 3 callouts, run in parallel. The callback runs once after all return. The max timeout is 120 seconds.

questions.q: A before-update trigger fires in a synchronous transaction started by a user clicking Save. How many SOQL queries can the whole transaction issue before a `LimitException`?
questions.explain: A user clicking Save starts a synchronous transaction, and sync Apex gets 100 SOQL queries. Every trigger, flow-called Apex and class in that transaction shares those 100. Think: one wallet for the whole trip.
wrong: 50 is the cap on `@future` calls per transaction, not on queries.
150 is the DML statement limit, not the query limit.
200 is the async query limit, and this transaction is synchronous.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A Batch Apex `execute()` method builds a large in-memory map and fails with a heap error. Per the current Execution Governors and Limits page, what heap limit is it working against?
options: 25 MB
10 MB
100 MB
60 MB
questions.explain: Batch Apex is async, so each `execute()` gets the async heap of 25 MB. Sync code gets only 10 MB. Older guides say 6 MB / 12 MB; current docs say 10 MB / 25 MB.
wrong: 10 MB is the sync heap, but Batch Apex runs async.
No Apex heap limit is 100 MB.
60 is the async CPU limit in seconds, not a heap size.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A shared utility method runs an optional enrichment query. It is called from triggers, batch jobs and LWC controllers. The developer wants it to skip the query when the transaction has no SOQL budget left. What should they do?
options: Wrap the query in `try/catch` and ignore `System.LimitException`.
Call `OrgLimits.getMap()` and skip the query when `DailyApiRequests` shows no remaining calls.
Hard-code a counter that stops after 100 queries.
Check `Limits.getQueries()` against `Limits.getLimitQueries()` first.
questions.explain: Ask the platform what is left instead of guessing. `Limits.getQueries()` is what you used, and `Limits.getLimitQueries()` is the cap for this context (100 sync, 200 async). So the same check works everywhere.
wrong: A `LimitException` can't be caught, so `try/catch` never runs.
`OrgLimits` covers org-wide limits like daily API calls, not this transaction's queries.
A fixed 100 is wrong in async code (200) and ignores queries other code already ran.
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: Limits Class

questions.q: A developer moves heavy logic from a trigger into a Queueable job. Which two limits are higher in the Queueable than in the synchronous trigger? Choose 2.
options: Total SOQL queries
Total DML statements
Maximum CPU time
Total rows retrieved by SOQL
Total callouts
questions.explain: Moving to async raises only the "brain" limits. SOQL goes from 100 to 200, and CPU goes from 10,000 ms to 60,000 ms. Heap also rises, from 10 MB to 25 MB.
wrong: DML statements stay at 150 in sync and async.
Query rows stay at 50,000 in sync and async.
Callouts stay at 100 in sync and async.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A data load of 200 Contacts fails with "Too many SOQL queries: 101". What is the best fix?
options: Move the lookup into a `@future` method called once per Contact so each query runs in its own transaction.
Add `LIMIT 1` to the query inside the loop.
Collect AccountIds in a Set, run one query into a `Map<Id, Account>`, then loop and read from the map.
Ask the admin to load Contacts in batches of 100.
questions.explain: Never query inside a loop. Gather the AccountIds, run one query into a `Map<Id, Account>`, then read from the map. That is one query whether 1 or 200 Contacts arrive.
wrong: You get only 50 `@future` calls, and a before trigger's field change would be lost in a future method.
`LIMIT 1` still runs one query per record.
Smaller batches hide the bug; the API or UI can still send 200 records.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Bulk Apex Triggers

questions.q: A nightly process reads about 40,000 Case records and its heap usage is near the limit. What does switching to a SOQL for loop that iterates over `List<Case>` batches achieve?
options: It removes the 50,000 query row limit.
It runs the query asynchronously on another thread.
It lets the code run DML inside the loop on each chunk without counting against the 150-statement limit.
It retrieves records in chunks of 200, so the full result set is never held in heap at once.
questions.explain: A SOQL for loop reads records in chunks of 200, so only one chunk sits in memory. That cuts heap use. It uses `queryMore` behind the scenes.
wrong: Every row still counts toward the 50,000-row limit.
The loop runs in the same transaction, not on another thread.
DML inside the loop still counts toward the 150-statement limit.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Working with Very Large SOQL Queries

questions.q: A developer needs fast lookups of Accounts by Id for records in `Trigger.new`. Which snippet is the most efficient?
options: Loop through a `List<Account>` each time a Contact needs its Account.
`Map<Id, Account> m = new Map<Id, Account>([SELECT Id, Name FROM Account WHERE Id IN :ids]);`
Query each Account inside the Contact loop with `WHERE Id = :c.AccountId`.
Use `Database.query()` with a string built inside the loop.
questions.explain: For fast lookups, use a Map. Passing a query result to the Map constructor builds an Id-keyed map in one query. Each lookup is then instant.
wrong: Scanning a list for every Contact is a nested loop that burns CPU.
One query per record breaks the 100-query limit.
Dynamic SOQL in a loop still runs one query per pass.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Maps of sObjects

questions.q: An after-insert trigger on Opportunity recalculates a `Total_Won__c` field on the parent Account. A 200-record load hits limits. Which two changes improve the code? Choose 2.
options: Call a `@future` method once per Opportunity so each Account update runs in its own transaction with fresh limits.
Replace the per-record query with one aggregate query: `SUM(Amount) GROUP BY AccountId` for all affected AccountIds.
Use `Database.update(acc, false)` instead of `update`.
Collect Account records in a `Map<Id, Account>` and issue a single update after the loop.
Add `LIMIT 200` to the inner query.
questions.explain: Do the math in the database and save once. One aggregate query, `SUM(Amount) GROUP BY AccountId`, replaces up to 200 queries. A Map of Accounts removes duplicates and allows one update.
wrong: Up to 200 `@future` calls blows past the limit of 50 per transaction.
`allOrNone=false` changes how errors are handled, not how many DML statements run.
`LIMIT` doesn't cut the number of queries and could make totals wrong.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Bulk Apex Triggers; Aggregate Functions

questions.q: Which field on a custom object is indexed by default, with no help from Support?
options: A custom Text field
`CreatedDate`
A custom Picklist field like `Stage__c`
A Long Text Area field
questions.explain: Some fields come indexed for free. `CreatedDate` is one, along with `Id`, `Name`, `OwnerId`, `SystemModstamp`, `RecordTypeId` and relationship fields.
wrong: A custom text field is indexed only if marked External ID or Unique, or by Support.
Picklists aren't indexed by default.
Long Text Area fields can't be indexed at all.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Working with Very Large SOQL Queries

questions.q: An object has 2,000,000 records. A query filters only on a custom field that has a custom index, and the filter matches 250,000 records. How will the optimizer most likely treat this filter?
options: Selective, because 250,000 is under the 333,333 cap.
Selective, because 250,000 is under 30% of 2,000,000.
Not selective, because the custom index threshold for 2M rows is 150,000 records.
Not selective, because custom indexes are never used on objects over 1M records.
questions.explain: A custom index works only under its threshold: 10% of the first 1M rows plus 5% of the rest. Here that is 100,000 + 50,000 = 150,000. The filter matches 250,000, so the index is skipped.
wrong: 333,333 is only the top cap; the real threshold here is lower.
30% is for standard indexes, not custom ones.
Custom indexes do work on big objects when the filter is selective enough.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Working with Very Large SOQL Queries

questions.q: An object has 500,000 records. A report query filters on `CreatedDate = LAST_N_DAYS:90`, which matches 120,000 rows. Is the filter selective?
options: Yes. `CreatedDate` has a standard index, and 120,000 is under 30% of 500,000.
No. Date filters are never selective.
No. 120,000 is above 10% of 500,000 (50,000), the selectivity threshold for this filter.
Yes, but only if the query has an `ORDER BY` clause.
questions.explain: `CreatedDate` has a standard index, and a standard index allows up to 30% of the first 1M rows. For 500,000 rows that is 150,000. The filter matches 120,000, so it is selective.
wrong: Indexed date fields can be selective.
10% is the custom-index threshold, but `CreatedDate` is a standard index.
`ORDER BY` has nothing to do with selectivity.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Working with Very Large SOQL Queries

questions.q: A trigger queries `Shipment__c` (5 million rows) with `WHERE Tracking_Code__c = :code`. `Tracking_Code__c` is a plain, non-indexed Text field, and the trigger fails with a non-selective query error. Which two actions can fix it? Choose 2.
options: Add `ORDER BY Tracking_Code__c` to the query.
Mark `Tracking_Code__c` as an External ID so it is indexed.
Change the filter to `LIKE '%' + code`.
Add another selective, indexed filter such as a lookup Id or a narrow `CreatedDate` range that matches the business rule.
Rewrite the query as dynamic SOQL with `Database.query()` so the optimizer builds a fresh plan for each call.
questions.explain: A trigger query needs a selective indexed filter. Marking the field External ID gives it a custom index. Adding another selective indexed filter works too.
wrong: Sorting doesn't make a filter selective.
A leading wildcard blocks the index.
Dynamic SOQL goes through the same optimizer, so nothing changes.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Working with Very Large SOQL Queries

questions.q: In the Developer Console Query Plan tool, the best plan for a query shows a Cost of 2.4. What does this mean?
options: The query uses 2.4 seconds of CPU time.
The query is selective and will use an index.
The query will consume 2.4% of the SOQL row limit.
The query is not selective; the optimizer expects it to be slow.
questions.explain: In the Query Plan tool, the line is 1. A cost above 1 means not selective, so the optimizer expects a slow query. Selective plans cost less than 1.
wrong: Cost is a relative score, not seconds.
A selective plan costs less than 1, not 2.4.
Cost has nothing to do with governor limits.
questions.source: Developer Console Query Plan Tool FAQ

questions.q: `Name` is indexed on Account. Which `WHERE` clause is least able to use that index?
options: `Name = 'Acme Corp'`
`Name IN ('Acme', 'Globex')`
`Name LIKE '%corp'`
`Name LIKE 'Acme%'`
questions.explain: An index is sorted from the start of the value, like a dictionary. A leading wildcard (`%corp`) gives it no start to look up, so it scans. A trailing wildcard (`Acme%`) can still use the index.
wrong: Exact equality on an indexed field can use the index.
`IN` with a short list can use the index.
A trailing wildcard still lets the index scan by prefix.
questions.source: Query & Search Optimization Cheat Sheet

questions.q: A query on a 3M-row object filters `WHERE Region__c = null`. `Region__c` has a custom index, but the query is slow. What explains it and what helps?
options: Custom indexes exclude nulls by default. Ask Support for an index that includes nulls, or store a default value instead.
Null filters are always selective on custom-indexed fields, so the slowness must come from network latency or page rendering.
`Region__c` must be converted to a formula field to be indexed.
The index only works when the query uses SOSL.
questions.explain: Custom indexes leave out nulls by default, so `= null` can't use them. Ask Support for an index that includes nulls, or store a default value instead.
wrong: Null filters on custom-indexed fields are a classic cause of full table scans.
Formula fields are harder to index, not easier.
SOSL uses the search index, not field indexes, so it doesn't help here.
questions.source: Best Practices for Deployments with Large Data Volumes

questions.q: Reports on a 20M-row custom object are slow because they always read the same 12 fields, and the object's standard and custom fields live in separate tables. A skinny table is proposed. Which statement is accurate?
options: A developer can create it in Setup and add parent Account fields to it.
Salesforce Support creates it, and the platform keeps it in sync with the source object.
It is copied to every sandbox type automatically on refresh.
It removes the need for selective filters, because every query against a skinny table is treated as indexed.
questions.explain: Only Salesforce Support can create a skinny table. It holds fields from one object so reads skip a join. The platform keeps it in sync for you.
wrong: Developers can't create skinny tables, and they can't hold fields from other objects.
They copy over automatically only to Full sandboxes.
Skinny tables cut joins, but filters still need to be selective.
questions.source: Best Practices for Deployments with Large Data Volumes

questions.q: At roughly what point does Salesforce consider a single user to have ownership skew on an object?
options: More than 1,000 records
More than 2,000 records
More than 10,000 records
More than 1,000,000 records
questions.explain: Skew starts when one user owns more than about 10,000 records of one object. That is Salesforce's line for ownership skew.
wrong: 1,000 records is too few to cause skew problems.
2,000 is the SOSL row limit, not a skew line.
Problems start long before 1,000,000 records.
questions.source: Designing Record Access for Enterprise Scale

questions.q: An integration user owns 400,000 Account records. Each time the admin moves that user to a different role, sharing recalculation runs for hours. What should the architect recommend?
options: Give the integration user the System Administrator profile.
Split the Accounts into two record types.
Change the Account OWD to Public Read/Write and move the user into a mid-level role under the sales VP.
Assign the user no role, or an isolated role at the top of the hierarchy, and avoid changing it.
questions.explain: Keep a skewed owner out of the hierarchy's way. With no role, or a lone role at the top, role changes don't force huge sharing recalculations.
wrong: Profile permissions don't change sharing recalculation from role moves.
Record types have nothing to do with ownership-based sharing.
Opening the OWD is a big security change, and a mid-level role keeps the recalculation problem.
questions.source: Designing Record Access for Enterprise Scale

questions.q: A nightly Bulk API job loads 3 million `Order__c` records that look up to a small set of Account records. Many batches fail with `UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW`. Which two actions reduce the errors? Choose 2.
options: Increase the number of parallel batches so the job finishes faster.
Sort the load file by the parent Account Id so each batch touches fewer parents.
Disable field history tracking on Account.
Switch the job to serial mode if sorting is not enough.
Add a trigger that retries failed records synchronously.
questions.explain: Locks come from parallel batches saving children of the same parent. Sorting by parent Id groups each parent's children together. Serial mode stops the batches from fighting at all.
wrong: More parallel batches means more fights over the same locks.
Field history tracking has nothing to do with parent row locks.
Retrying in a trigger adds load and hits the same locks again.
questions.source: Bulk API 2.0 Developer Guide; Best Practices for Deployments with Large Data Volumes

questions.q: A company is about to restructure its role hierarchy and add many sharing rules, then reload 2M records. How can they reduce the time spent on sharing recalculation?
options: Run the changes in a Queueable to get higher limits.
Use the Defer Sharing Calculations feature, make the changes, then resume and recalculate once.
Temporarily delete all sharing rules, reload the data, and recreate the rules later from a metadata backup.
Make every user a System Administrator during the load.
questions.explain: Pause the sharing math during big changes. Defer Sharing Calculations holds recalculation until you resume. Then it runs once instead of after every change.
wrong: Apex limits don't control the platform's sharing recalculation.
Deleting and recreating rules is risky and still triggers recalculation.
Making everyone an admin is a security risk and doesn't stop recalculation.
questions.source: Best Practices for Deployments with Large Data Volumes

questions.q: In one transaction, several trigger handlers call `SettingsCache.getRates()`. What does the pattern below achieve?
options: It caches the rates for all users for 24 hours, like the Platform Cache org partition.
It makes the query run asynchronously.
It runs the query once per transaction and reuses the map on later calls.
It removes the query from the 50,000 row limit.
questions.explain: A static variable lives for one transaction. The first call queries and fills the map. Every later call in that transaction gets the same map with no new query.
wrong: Statics reset every transaction; sharing across users needs Platform Cache.
The query runs right away on the first call, not in the background.
The rows still count toward the 50,000 limit, just once.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Static and Instance Methods, Variables

questions.q: Currency rates come from an external service, change once a day, and are needed by every user on many pages. Which approach best reduces repeated callouts?
options: Store the rates in a static variable in the controller.
Cache the rates in the Platform Cache org partition with a TTL; call the service only on a miss.
Store the rates in the Platform Cache session partition so each user's pages read them without a new callout.
Store the rates in the Visualforce view state.
questions.explain: Data that everyone needs belongs in the org cache. It is shared by all users across transactions. One callout serves everyone until the TTL (time to live) runs out.
wrong: A static variable lasts only one transaction.
Session cache is per user, so every user would make their own callout.
View state belongs to one page instance and just bloats the page.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Platform Cache

questions.q: A developer reads a value from Platform Cache and immediately uses it. Testing passes, but production sometimes throws a `NullPointerException`. What is the most likely reason?
questions.code:
Decimal eur = (Decimal) Cache.Org.get('local.Rates.EUR');
Decimal converted = amount * eur;
options: Org cache is only available in asynchronous Apex.
The key format is invalid; Platform Cache keys must always start with `"c."` instead of `"local."` in every org.
Cache values are always returned as strings.
Cached items can expire or be evicted at any time, so the code must handle a null and reload.
questions.explain: Platform Cache is best effort: items can expire or be pushed out at any time. So always check for null and reload the value. `Cache.CacheBuilder` can do that reload for you.
wrong: Org cache works in both sync and async Apex.
Keys use `namespace.partition.key`, and `local` is correct for an org with no namespace.
`get()` returns the stored `Object`, which you can cast.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Platform Cache Best Practices

questions.q: A before-update trigger hits "Apex CPU time limit exceeded" on bulk updates. The code calls `Schema.getGlobalDescribe()` inside a loop and uses nested for loops to match Contacts to Accounts. Which two changes most reduce CPU time? Choose 2.
options: Replace the nested loops with a `Map<Id, List<Contact>>` built in one pass.
Add `System.debug` statements to find the slow line in production.
Get describe information once (for example `Contact.SObjectType.getDescribe()`) and store it in a static variable.
Move the matching logic into a SOQL query inside the loop, because database time is not counted.
Convert the trigger to an after-update trigger.
questions.explain: CPU burns on repeated work. A Map built in one pass replaces the nested loops. Describing once and keeping the result in a static stops repeated describe calls.
wrong: More debug statements add CPU time, not remove it.
A query in a loop breaks the 100-query limit.
An after trigger does the same work and needs extra DML.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits; Apex Developer Guide: Understanding Apex Describe Information

questions.q: A Lightning web component uses `@wire` to call an Apex method that returns a list of Accounts. What must the Apex method have?
options: `@RemoteAction`
`@AuraEnabled` only
`@AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)`
`@InvocableMethod`
questions.explain: `@wire` only calls Apex marked safe to cache. That means `@AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)`, which also turns on client-side caching.
wrong: `@RemoteAction` is for Visualforce JavaScript remoting.
Without `cacheable=true`, a method can only be called imperatively.
`@InvocableMethod` is for Flow, not for LWC.

questions.q: A `lightning-datatable` must let users scroll through up to 50,000 Case records. Loading all of them at once freezes the page. What is the best approach?
options: Return all 50,000 rows from a cacheable method so the client caches them.
Use infinite loading: `onloadmore` fetches the next 50 rows with keyset paging (`WHERE Id > :lastId ORDER BY Id`).
Use SOQL `OFFSET` in the `onloadmore` handler to fetch the next 50 rows each time, all the way down to the 50,000th row.
Render 50,000 rows with a `for:each` template instead of the datatable.
questions.explain: Load a small page at a time as the user scrolls. Infinite loading fetches 50 rows on each `loadmore`. Keyset paging (`WHERE Id > :lastId`) works at any depth, unlike `OFFSET`.
wrong: 50,000 rows still overload the browser and the payload, cached or not.
SOQL `OFFSET` is capped at 2,000 rows.
Drawing 50,000 rows by hand is even slower.
questions.source: Lightning Component Library: lightning-datatable; SOQL and SOSL Reference: OFFSET

questions.q: A search box in an LWC calls an Apex search method on every keystroke, causing many server round trips. What should the developer do?
options: Mark the Apex method `cacheable=false`.
Move the search into `renderedCallback()`.
Switch the Apex method to `@future` so the searches run in the background and stop blocking the user's typing.
Debounce: restart a `setTimeout` on each keystroke and call Apex only after the user pauses (about 300 ms).
questions.explain: Wait until the user stops typing. Debouncing restarts a short timer on each keystroke and calls Apex only after a pause of about 300 ms. One call replaces many.
wrong: Turning off caching makes the server load worse.
`renderedCallback` runs after every render and can cause loops.
A `@future` method can't return data to a component.
questions.source: LWC Recipes: Debounce; Trailhead: Performance Troubleshooting in LWC

questions.q: A record page loads slowly. It contains a custom LWC with four tabs, each with a heavy child component, and each child uses its own imperative Apex call to read fields from the current record. Which two changes improve performance? Choose 2.
options: Call `refreshApex()` every few seconds to keep the data fresh.
Render each tab's heavy child only when that tab is active, using `lwc:if`.
Mark the Apex methods `cacheable=true` and also have them update a "Last Viewed" field.
Load all four children in `connectedCallback()` so they are ready early.
Read the current record's fields with Lightning Data Service (`getRecord`) so components share one cache instead of separate Apex calls.
questions.explain: Build only what users see, and share data. `lwc:if` builds a tab's heavy child only when that tab is open. LDS (`getRecord`) caches the record once for every component.
wrong: Polling with `refreshApex` adds server load.
Cacheable methods can't do DML, so the "Last Viewed" update fails.
Loading everything up front is exactly what makes the page slow.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Lightning Data Service; Conditional Rendering

questions.q: What is the maximum view state size for a Visualforce page?
options: 170 KB
135 KB
6 MB
1 MB
questions.explain: Visualforce view state can be at most 170 KB. Bigger pages fail with a view state error.
wrong: 135 KB is not the Visualforce limit.
6 MB is the old sync Apex heap size, not a view state limit.
1 MB is not the view state limit.

questions.q: A Visualforce controller builds a large `List<ChartPoint>` for a chart. The list is rebuilt on every request anyway, but it makes the view state huge. What should the developer do?
options: Move the list into a controller extension instead of the main controller.
Move the list into a hidden `apex:inputText`.
Declare the list with the `transient` keyword.
Ask Salesforce Support to raise the view state limit.
